title: Dozens of warrantless arrests deemed wrongful in class-action immigration case
text:
Montana Free Press

Montana's independent nonprofit news source.

Your state. Know what's shaping Montana.

From community meetings to federal policies, MTFP reporting answers critical questions across the state.

Attorneys at Helena-based Upper Seven Law have been filing petitions for the release of dozens of immigration detainees.

The firm filed 37 last week and, as of midday Monday, it had presented six more to the court amid a flurry of paperwork.

The release of detainees came in a batch, too. Upper Seven announced last Friday that 24 “unlawfully detained individuals” had been released from the Cascade County Detention Center. More are expected to be released as the court considers more petitions, Andres Haladay, an attorney with Upper Seven, told Montana Free Press Monday.

Under court orders, federal authorities identified 53 people who met the court’s criteria for being wrongfully detained. Two were children — one as young as 9 — and have already been released.

All of this came after U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris granted class status to people who were arrested by immigration authorities in Montana without warrants and remained in detention without any determination of whether they presented a flight risk. The class members have little or no criminal history and were often arrested during traffic stops initiated by local law enforcement agencies. Immigration laws didn’t require mandatory detention, the judge wrote, but were treated as such.

In court documents, detainees described being swept up in traffic stops and then placed in unsafe or uncomfortable detention conditions. One said he thought he passed out in the back of a box truck from the heat. Another said that a Border Patrol agent kicked him in the back before discouraging him from speaking to anyone, including an attorney.

Judge Morris concluded that federal authorities wrongfully arrested and detained these people. On Sept. 15, he issued another order declaring that the government violated the prior order by keeping these people in detention and approved release orders for the first 24 detainees days later.

In an emailed statement on Friday, a spokesperson for U.S. Customs and Border Protection said the agency was awaiting individual release petitions and that it “is complying with the court’s order regarding release.”

The class certification for the Montana defendants was based on successful release petitions in individual cases such as that of Roberto Orozco Ramirez, a mechanic who lives in the small town of Froid. Judge Morris also presided over that case and lamented the lack of due process for the immigration detainees.

The use of release petitions, through a process called habeas corpus, has exploded during the second Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

“We have to start from the standpoint that a little over a year and a half ago, there was no need for any of this,” Haladay said. “Overzealous immigration enforcement didn’t exist.”

Haladay said that as Upper Seven and other law firms addressed habeas cases individually, detainees were being moved from state to state, prolonging the court process and straining defendants’ families.

This latest class action prevents the government from moving those people out of Montana.

“You can see the scale of how many people are having their rights violated and how many people need help and access to the courts who don’t get served through those one-offs,” Haladay said.

The release of 24 people on Friday coincided with the Cascade County sheriff’s announcement that a critical staffing shortage necessitated reducing the jail population. The Cascade County Detention Center has been a holding facility for many immigrants going through the court process, and federal detention contracts are a major source of revenue for the facility.

“I recognize the importance of our federal, state and local partnerships, but my first responsibility is ensuring the Cascade County Detention Center can operate safely,” Sheriff Jesse Slaughter wrote in a press release late last week. “We simply do not have enough personnel right now to safely maintain the population we have been housing.”

The court will continue to consider expedited release petitions in the class-action case, Haladay said. Morris asked the federal government to consider at least five petitions per day if it wishes to challenge the release of any of the detainees.

This story was updated on Sept. 22, 2026, to correct the agency title for U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

General election voters in Butte-Silver Bow County may now consider a proposed ballot initiative that would require citizen approval of data center development, after the Montana Supreme Court overturned a lower court ruling that prevented the initiative from appearing on the November ballot. In a court filing responding to the decision, the county said it intends to comply, but is unsure of how to follow the ruling and remain in compliance with the Montana Election Code, since ballots have already been printed — and some have already been sent and returned — without the initiative.

County commissioners passed effort unanimously after three-year campaign by local organizers.

11th District Court judges Amy Eddy and Dan Wilson are competing for the state Supreme Court in an unusual race between two judges from the same court. But more interesting than the commonality of the candidates’ current jobs is the politicized flavor of the nominally nonpartisan race. Adding to the race’s ideological dynamic, the campaigns’ partisan overtones are playing out as Montanans will consider on the same November ballot a constitutional initiative — CI-132 — that would require judicial races in Montana to remain nonpartisan, as they have been for decades.

Matt Hudson has covered Great Falls for MTFP Local since 2024. He also writes Great Falls This Week, a recurring newsletter about local issues. He is a graduate of the University of Montana School of Journalism, and previously worked as a reporter for the Owatonna People's Press, in Minnesota, the Daily Inter Lake in Kalispell and the Billings Gazette.
